subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Strategic Voting
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Strategic Voting.

hook.text: You prefer candidate A but vote for B because only B can beat C, whom you dislike most.

buildup.text: Strategic voting means voting for a less-preferred candidate who has a better chance of winning against your.

discovery.text: Gibbard and Satterthwaite proved no voting system is immune to strategic manipulation.

twist.text: Polls enable strategic voting by revealing who can win. Without polls, voters express true preferences more often.

climax.text: Voting systems shape strategy. Ranked-choice reduces strategic voting by letting you express a true first choice safely.

punchline.text: Every voting system can be gamed. The best ones make gaming unnecessary.

quiz.question: What did the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem prove?
options: Some voting systems are perfectly fair
No voting system is completely immune to strategic manipulation
Strategic voting always produces the best outcomes

details.summary: Strategic voting occurs when voters choose a candidate other than their true preference to influence the election outcome, such as voting for the lesser evil to prevent the worst outcome rather than supporting the most-preferred but unviable candidate.
details.whyItMatters: Strategic voting undermines the ideal of elections reflecting true preferences. Understanding voting as a game reveals why third parties struggle, why polls influence behavior, and why electoral system design matters so much.
takeaways: Voters often choose strategically rather than sincerely in elections
First-past-the-post systems incentivize the most strategic voting
Polls serve as coordination devices that enable strategic behavior

faq.question: Is strategic voting rational?
faq.answer: Yes, given the incentives of the electoral system. In first-past-the-post systems, voting for a third-party candidate who cannot win effectively wastes your vote. Strategically supporting a viable second choice has more impact.

faq.question: Do different voting systems reduce strategic behavior?
faq.answer: Some systems like ranked-choice voting reduce the incentive to vote strategically because ranking your true favorite first is less risky. But no voting system completely eliminates strategic incentives, as proven by the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem.
